slides.headline: 891 wild lions. One corner of India.
slides.sub: Gir and the land around it are the Asiatic lion's last refuge

slides.headline: They once roamed from Syria to Bihar
slides.body: Lions ranged across south-west Asia and much of northern and central India. Heavy hunting and habitat loss left them only in Gujarat's Gir Forest.

slides.label: lions counted in May 2025, up from 284 in 1990
slides.body: That is a 32% rise since the 2020 estimate of 674, and over 70% growth in a decade.

slides.headline: Spreading beyond Gir
slides.body: Lions now roam about 35,000 km² across 11 districts of Saurashtra. In 2023 they reached Barda Wildlife Sanctuary, returning after 143 years.

slides.headline: Still Endangered
slides.body: IUCN lists the lion species as Vulnerable (2023). The Asiatic subpopulation is listed separately as Endangered, an assessment dating from 2008.

caption:
Every wild Asiatic lion (Panthera leo, Asiatic subpopulation) lives in one corner of India: Gir and Saurashtra, Gujarat.

The May 2025 count found 891 lions, up from 674 in 2020 and 284 in 1990. One of the newest homes is Barda Wildlife Sanctuary, 192 km² across Porbandar and Devbhumi Dwarka, where lions arrived on their own in 2023 and now number 17, including 11 cubs.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Press Information Bureau, Government of India (2025); IUCN Red List.

Pass this on to someone planning a trip to Gujarat.
